### **MARKET DEVELOPMENTS** 

_Volatile trading conditions during the first half of May_ 

_Prices supported by industrial action at Lomas Bayas_ 

_Market sentiment dampened by falling equity markets_ 

During the first half of May trading conditions were particularly volatile with daily min/max variations in 3-month quotes ranging from -$226/t to +$182/t.  The volatility reflected mixed sentiment which was reflected in LME open interest data during this period.  The data indicates that new long positions, long liquidation and the establishment of new short positions were responsible for this price volatility.  As a consequence, official 3-month quotes rose from $4491/t at the end of April to $4778/t on the 7<sup>th</sup> before falling by $455/t to $4323/t on the 14<sup>th</sup> , which was the month’s low. 

The $287/t gain in price (3m) during the first week in May reflected the release of positive economic data and news of industrial action at Xstrata’s 70kt/a Lomas Bayas SxEw mine in Chile.  On the economic front, US construction spending rose in March (+0.3% month-on-month) for the first time in six months while pending home sales jumped 3.2% from a month earlier as buyers were encouraged by favourable house prices and loan mortgage rates.  This news was particularly encouraging because no sustained US economic recovery will occur until there is stability within the domestic construction sector.  Also supportive was the news that Chinese manufacturing activity in April continued to expand for the second consecutive month (see Consumption) while Chinese car sales, in the same month, jumped 37% year on year.  It appears that the government’s recent tax cuts and rebates are having a positive impact with the potential for further growth in the coming months.  Workers at Xstrata’s Lomas Bayas mine started industrial action on the 6<sup>th</sup> after unions failed to agree a 6% pay rise with management. 

However, industrial action at the mine was relatively short lived with workers returning to their jobs on the 15<sup>th</sup> .  This, combined with falling equity markets, dampened market sentiment during the second week of May which resulted in official 3-month quotes dropping to $4323/t on the 14<sup>th</sup> .  Equity markets were weakened by the news that US unemployment had reached 8.9% in April, its highest level since 1983, as well as lower than expected US retail sales which declined by 10.1% year on year and by 0.4% from March.  Auto and electronic sales were particularly weak, with motor vehicle and parts sales down by 20.7% in April from a year earlier.

_Page 2_ _May 2009_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ Since the 14th prices have recovered and are trading around $4800/t at the time of writing. In the absence of any fundamental news prices have strengthened on the back of a depreciating US dollar and stronger equity markets which were supported by the release of brighter economic data. The most notable was better than expected US consumer confidence, which surged to 54.9 in May from 39.2 a month earlier. During the second half of the month LME open interest data highlighted the extent to which the fund community had turned more positive towards copper. Between the 15th and 22nd LME open interest declined by 13.3k lots which, in tandem with a $268/t gain in price, suggested that short covering had contributed to the price increase (3m) which hit $4560/t on the 26th . For the month to-date (as of the 28th ) official 3-month quotes averaged $4570/t. This is up by 3.4% from April’s average of $4418/t and is the highest monthly average since October last year. On the physical side, total exchange stocks continued to decline during May, falling by a net 68kt to 396.5kt through to the 27th . Despite the overall decline in exchange inventories, Comex and SHFE warehouses actually increased by a net 5.5kt and 15.2kt, to 49.1kt and 30.2kt respectively. The rise in SHFE inventories was the largest monthly gain since February last year. Further increases are expected in the coming weeks with imports remaining at record levels at a time when demand is seasonally slower. Elsewhere, LME inventories continued to fall, by a net 88.7kt to 317.1kt. This represented the third consecutive month of decline reflecting the ongoing relocation of metal into China, attracted by higher prices and premia (albeit not as large as in previous months). The majority of withdrawals were from European locations where stocks fell by a net 44.1kt to 92.8kt. Cancelled warrants also declined during the month, falling from 83.1kt at the end of April to 43.7kt as of the 27th . Although these are not as high as in previous months they still indicate that further withdrawals will take place in the coming weeks. European premia strengthened during the month, reflecting buying activity in Asia rather than any meaningful recovery in European demand. Chinese buying has eased in recent weeks, partly reflecting a narrower SHFE/LME arbitrage, but market participants still prefer to ship metal into Asian warehouses and wait for more favourable arbitrage opportunities

_May 2009_ _Page 3_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ There have also been reports of a small improvement in underlying European consumption during the month, spurring the belief by some that the decline in demand actually bottomed out in March. The combination of this and the redirecting of metal to China has seen Chilean and Grade A material from Rotterdam trading up from $40-50/t in April to $75-90/t this month. Italian warrants have risen to between $80-90/t, compared with $50-70/t last month, while standard grade material increased by $10/t to $10-20/t. The latter continued to be supported by tightness in the scrap market. _..while US and Chinese premia weaken_ _SHFE/LME arbitrage narrowed during the month_ _The strength of the copper market thus far in 2009 has surprised many_ In the US, premia eased during the month, from 5-6c/lb in April to 4.5-5.5c/lb currently, reflecting quieter spot activity and a slowdown in Chinese buying. Likewise in China, premia for imported metal weakened during the month in tandem with a narrowing of the SHFE/LME price arbitrage. The shift in the arbitrage was prompted by the growing abundance of metal on account of the record level of imports in recent months. Chinese premia slipped form a peak of $160/t in April to $130-$150/t in May. As of the 26th SHFE prices traded at an average $173/t (net of VAT) above LME quotes. This compared with an average of $428/t in April, $203/t in March and $222/t in February. As a consequence, refined imports are expected to slow in June. However, in the meantime imports will remain robust due to the arbitragedriven orders that were made in recent months. Latest trade data showed Chinese refined copper imports increased by 148.4% in April year on year, to a new monthly record of 318kt. This followed an annual increase of 138% in March, to 297kt, and a 99% rise in February to 271kt. For the first four months of the year refined imports totalled ~1.1Mt, up by 106% over the corresponding period in 2008. Thus far in 2009 the relative strength of the copper market has been a surprise to many, including ourselves. However, there are concerns that China’s metal purchases have been far higher than their consumption requirements and that this will inevitably lead to a substantial slowdown in imports during the second half of the year. Ind

eed, apparent Chinese refined consumption growth in the first four months of 2009 rose by 40% year on year which, by any stretch of the imagination, is well in excess of market requirements. In fact, each year China typically buys far more metal than can be consumed during the period December through March. This mirrors arbitrage opportunities in favour of the SHFE that typically arise between Q4 and mid February of each year. WEEKLY COPPER EXCHANGE STOCKS AND CASH LME PRICE

_Page 4_ _May 2009_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ This is a self-fulfilling cycle because excessive cathode purchases at the start of each year is compounded by a marked rise in scrap availability/imports from March onwards, which floods the Chinese market with metal units, leading to a significant reversal in the arbitrage in favour of LME throughout the second and third quarters of each year as these stocks are worked off. The difference in 2009 is that scrap imports have failed to recover (i.e. imports were down by 25% year on year in April and down by 41% year on year in January-April period) and copper prices are also far lower than in recent years. Semis fabricators have thus been compelled to purchase more primary metal and, with easy credit and far lower prices, this has encouraged consumers to hold more stock. These factors have extended the positive arbitrage window by at least two months. If one assumes that scrap accounts for, say, 25% of overall Chinese semis production and also that scrap availability is down by 20%, then even if there is zero growth in semis output in 2009, a near 7% uplift in refined copper is still required just to offset the reduction in scrap. Because of the ongoing lack of scrap, we have raised our Chinese refined consumption growth figure from 8%, to 10% this year (see Consumption). And, while it seems unlikely that Chinese metal imports can be sustained at recent levels we believe that demand elsewhere will be less negative moving forward. The year-on-year collapse in consumption outside China in Q1 2009 was exacerbated by a very strong Q1 2008. Inventory adjustments (destocking) have also had a negative effect on demand thus far in 2009, although indications suggest that this factor is having far less effect of late and could, if anything, be a positive contributor to consumption during H2, even if demand picks up only moderately. Taking the above into account, we do not expect a major correction in price during H2 and are forecasting cash prices of $3775/t ($1.71/lb) compared with $3923/t ($1.78/lb)

in H1. For 2009 we are projecting an overall average of $3849/t ($1.75/lb). Next year, our forecast is for an 8.1% decline, to $3538/t ($1.60/lb) reflecting somewhat weaker market conditions due to an ongoing rise in metal inventories. However, in 2011 we expect a strong pick up in refined consumption along with declining inventories which is reflected in our price forecast of $3975/t ($1.80/lb). _Chinese Scrap imports normally strong from March onwards, not so in 2009_ _We have raised our Chinese demand forecast to reflect lower scrap supply_ _We do not forecast a major price correction during H2_ **PRICE FORECASTS AND WORLD QUARTERLY SUPPLY/DEMAND BALANCE – (kt)** |||**Refined**

### **CONSUMPTION** _We have revised our 2008 estimates_ _A sharp reduction in Kazakhstan copper demand is expected this year_ We have made a series of revisions to our 2008 estimates following the release of final reported consumption numbers for last year. Essentially we have lowered our estimates for France and Italy, where the downturn towards the latter part of last year was much stronger than we anticipated, and raised our figures for Brazil and Mexico. However, the net effect of these adjustments, alongside a few other revisions in Asia, was to leave our global demand number for last year unchanged at just below 18Mt. This represented annual growth of just 0.1%. Nevertheless, for this year, 2010 and 2011 we have raised our global demand forecasts since our last monthly report by 92kt, 186kt and 192kt respectively. The stronger forecasts reflect upward revisions to our Chinese figures where demand so far this year has been stronger than previously anticipated. Despite the overall increase in our near term demand forecasts, we have made a sharp reduction (-40kt) to our Kazakhstan demand forecasts. This followed Kazakhmys reporting an 84.3% (-~11kt) decline in wire rod production during Q1 from a year earlier. The company explained that it has reduced its production of copper wire rod because of the relatively low profit margins _Page 6_ _May 2009_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ compared with the margins that can be achieved from overseas cathode sales. Thus the company, currently, is only producing copper wire rod for the domestic market. Last year Kazakhmys produced 48kt of copper wire rod, up 35.3% from 2007, but this year we forecast that production will decline to just 9kt. Taking all of the revisions into account we forecast that global refined copper consumption will fall by 3.2% this year to just below 17.4Mt. Next year we project that demand will recover, increasing by 2.1% to ~17.8Mt, before rebounding strongly in 2011 to ~18.9Mt. This will represent an annual gain of 6.3%. During the month evidence that the global economy is stabilising continued to emerge. The latest source of encouragement came from the various purchasing managers’ index surveys which suggested that the pace of contraction is slowing in terms of manufacturing output. However, the PMIs for the US, the European Union and Japan were still below the levels seen at the bottom of the 2001 recession. PMIs are composite indices based on surveying manufacturing companies on variables such as production levels, order books, inventory levels, deliveries, employment and input prices. A reading above 50 indicates that manufacturing activity is expanding whereas a reading below suggests that activity is contracting. Therefore it was encouraging that China’s official PMI in April, at 53.5, stood above 50 for the second consecutive month. The reading reached a low of 38.8 in November last year an

d has been recovering steadily ever since. The new orders component of the April index was particularly strong at 56.6. This undoubtedly reflected the positive impact felt from the Government’s recent $585bn stimulus package. The stimulus package did benefit the demand for some white goods such as fridges, freezers and washing machines. According to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), production of these units rose by 7%, 5.2% and 2.3% respectively during the first four months of the year from the corresponding period in 2008. However, demand for air conditioners, which accounts for ~80% of copper demand from the appliance industry, remained weak from both the domestic and export markets. This was highlighted by the NBS reporting a 20.5% year on year decline in the output of air conditioners through to April. _Global demand forecast to fall by 3.2% this year_ _Evidence emerges to suggest that the global economy is stabilising_ _China’s PMI in April is encouraging_ _China’s stimulus package supporting demand for copper intensive white goods_ PURCHASING MANAGERS INDICES FOR MANUFACTURING

_May 2009_ _Page 7_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ _Chinese air conditioning market hampered by falling exports_ _China’s wire and cable sector performing well_ _Improvement in Japanese demand for rolled copper products seen in April…_ The Chinese air conditioning market has been heavily hampered by the global downturn in construction activity, particularly in the US. Exports of air conditioners declined by 36% year on year through to April. In an attempt to boost domestic sales of air conditioners, as well as other home appliances, China’s State Council recently unveiled a 2Bn Yuan ($293M) discount plan. The Council will fund discounts of fresh purchases of home appliances such as air conditioner units, televisions, fridges, washing machines etc. The aim of the plan is to help offset falling demand from the export markets. Elsewhere, in the wire and cable markets demand is extremely strong, reflecting increasing government investment within the power sector. According to official statistics, output of power cable increased by 35% year on year in Q1. Added to this our sources confirmed that some major wire and cable manufacturers have been operating at 90% of capacity since Q2 and have reported full order books for the remainder of the year. Reflecting the healthy market conditions Tianjin Dawufeng Copper Semis Co, which is owned by Tianjin Pipe Corporation (TPCO) recently announced that its second wire rod line (150kt/a) will be commissioned this month, lifting overall capacity at the plant to 300kt/a. In addition, Jiangrun Copper announced that strong demand from the wire and cable sector was pa

rtly responsible for the company’s planned output of copper wire rod rising to 240kt this year from 97kt in 2008. The ramping up of production at the company’s new 350kt/a wire rod line, which was commissioned last July, will also be responsible for the jump in production. Taking the above into account we continue to forecast that Chinese refined copper consumption will increase by 10% this year to ~5.5Mt. In Japan there are indications that the rate of decline in economic activity may be slowing. This was evidenced by industrial production rising by 1.6% in April from March, the first month-on-month increase since October last year. Meanwhile in the manufacturing sector the PMI for April reached above 40, also for the first time since October 2008. More importantly, however, the production of rolled copper products increased by ~29% in April from a month earlier, according to the Japan Copper and Brass Association. Once again this represented the first monthly increase since October last year. The increase mainly reflected a rise in demand for copper products from the auto and electronics sectors, especially for exports to China, and aggressive efforts by the brass mills to cut inventories of these products during the first three months of this year. Nevertheless, although the rise in April’s output was encouraging, production was down 48.6% from a year earlier. Worse still, year-to-date (JanApr) output fell by 53.3%from the corresponding period in 2008. JAPANESE PRODUCTION OF COPPER AND COPPER ALLOY PRODUCTS– (kt)

_Page 8_ _May 2009_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ There has been no sign of improvement in the wire and cable markets where the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association reported a 26.3% year on year decline in April shipments. This represented the seventh consecutive month of decline. Demand from the construction sector, which accounted for ~46% of total shipments, remained particularly weak with shipments falling by 18.1% from a year earlier. Orders from the construction sector continued to be hampered by the slowdown in economic activity and stricter building guidelines which were introduced during H2 2007. Other significant declines included shipments to the electrical and electronic and auto sectors which fell annually by 41.7% and 46.5% respectively. The latter reflected the ongoing slowdown in the auto sector where production dropped by 23.6% during Jan-Apr from a year earlier. Added to this, Toyota recently reported that it will sell 1M fewer vehicles this year due to the global economic crisis. According to the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association copper wire and cable shipments declined by 26.8% year on year thro

ugh to April. The Association also reported that it expects demand for copper wire and cable to fall to its lowest level in 34 years during the current fiscal year which runs from April this year to March 2010. With this in mind we forecast that Japanese refined copper consumption will weaken by 15.8% this year to ~1Mt. Elsewhere in Asia Nexans recently announced that it had signed a joint venture with Polycab, India’s largest cable company, to build a new cable production unit in India. The joint venture will cover the manufacture and marketing of special cables for the shipbuilding, material handling, railway and wind power industries as well as the production of high voltage underground cables. The venture will mark Nexan’s first industrial foothold in the Indian market where it hopes to benefit from the sustained growth of this emerging market. This particularly applies to the growing power infrastructure market. The new cable unit, which is expected to take between 12-18 months to build, bodes well for future copper demand. This is reflected in our forecast of 4.5% growth in Indian refined copper consumption next year, to ~620kt, followed by a 10.1% increase in 2011 to ~690kt. mand_ Meanwhile in Europe recent production results highlighted the extent of the slowdown in demand during Q1. The KME group, a major European producer of copper and copper alloy products, reported a 28% (-113.7kt) decline in output during Q1 from a year earlier. The company did not provide a product output breakdown but it did report that demand for brass rods used in plumbing was hit the hardest. This was not surprising in light of the slowdown in the European construction sector. In contrast, demand for products used in the power generation industry, especially in renewable energy generation, was more resilient. Elsewhere German copper producer, Aurubis, reported a 40% year on year (-23kt) decline in its production of copper and copper alloy strip products during Q1 and a 34.5% (-19kt) annual decline in its output of copper shapes during the three month period. In the wire rod market Aurubis reported that the decline that began in October last year continued through into 2009 but order intake did stabilise in March. Production at the group’s four wire rod plants totalled 168kt in March, which was up 5.7% from the December quarter. Unfortunately comparable numbers on an annual basis are not available due to Cumerio’s production figures having been included from March 2008. On a positive note, Aurubis recently observed that demand in May showed tentative signs of improvement. Despite this we forecast that European refined copper consumption will decline by 9.8% this year to just under 3.1Mt. Finally, in the US the ongoing slowdown in the US construction continued to impact negatively on demand for copper products. According to the Copper and Brass Servicenter Association, service centre shipments of copper and copper alloy products fell annually by 30.7% and 37.4% respectively in March. In the month shipments of copper sheet declined by 42.4%, copper rod fell by 22.1%, copper pipe was lower by 20% while copper plate declined by 11.8% from a year earlier. For Q1 as a whole, shipments of copper and copper alloy products fell by 35% year on year. With this in mind we continue to forecast a 10.1% decline in US refined copper consumption this year to 1.8Mt. ||**GLOBAL**

_Chinese concentrate imports rise marginally (+3.13%) during the first 4 months of 2009_ 

_Acid woes return to the Chinese smelting market_ 

_Over 200kt/a of incremental Chinese smelting capacity comes to light during May_ 

_Mid-year concentrate negotiations kick off in Asia although no terms are tabled_ 

At 518.9kdmt, China’s April 2009 copper concentrate imports registered a 2.87% year-on-year increase.  On a cumulative basis the figure for the first four months was 1.93Mdmt which represented a marginal (+3.13%) uplift on the same period in 2008.  As was the case in March, imports from Chile during April were considerably below last year’s level

(-44%) while an 80% increase from Australia meant that this country’s contribution was almost on a par with its Latin American counterpart. 

As noted, there are renewed concerns about the ability of smelters to sell their acid into an extremely lacklustre domestic market.  Fertilisers account for 70% of all acid consumption in China and producers of the former are now reportedly holding large inventories once more.  Export taxes on chemical fertilisers were raised from 35% to 100% in April last year as a means of lowering the domestic price for fertilisers in order to reduce basic food prices.  On December 1<sup>st</sup> 2008 the tax was lowered to 10% during the so-called “slack” season (January, June, July, November and December) and to 75% during all other months.  Poor demand for acid has led to a further reduction in prices, which are currently quoted at a little over $10/t in southern provinces. 

Over the past month three additional Chinese smelter projects have come to light which, collectively will contribute in excess of 200kt/a of incremental copper smelting capacity to the country’s existing total.  Construction of Liangshan Mining’s 100kt/a project in Sichuan province is reportedly progressing well and the company, a subsidiary of Yunnan Copper, aims to commission the $50M project by year end.  The Liangshan mine produces 1015kt/a of copper-in-concentrates and hence the new smelter will rely on imports for the balance of its requirements.  Elsewhere, Yunnan Tin Group has started construction of a 100kt/a smelter/refinery to replace its antiquated 25kt/a blister plant.  The new smelter, which will be based on Ausmelt technology, is due to be commissioned in June 2010 and will require approximately 300kt/a of imported concentrates to supplement local mine production.  China’s State Development Planning Commission has recently announced that it intends to shut 300kt/a of obsolete copper smelting capacity by the end of 2009 and Yunnan Tin’s old plant would fall under this category.  The third development is a 40kt/a smelter project, located in Yongxin County (Jiangxi province) that has just been put into trial production by Jinfeng Nonferrous Metals.  At this stage it remains unclear as to whether this plant is a primary or secondary smelter. 

The mid-year TC/RC negotiations began in earnest during May with BHP Billiton, acting on behalf of Escondida, entering into first round discussions with its Indian, Korean and Japanese counterparts.  It appears that no numbers were officially tabled at this stage although one might imagine that the Chilean miner will be looking for a roll-over of last year’s levels (i.e. in the low 40s & 4s) whereas smelting companies will be wanting numbers closer to the last annual Mating Season settlements (i.e. $75/t & 7.5c/lb).

The ongoing decline in primary smelter capacity utilisation rates (i.e. 78% estimated for 2009 compared with 81% in 2008 and 84% in 2007) could be seen as justification for a mid-year TC/RC number at the lower end of the miner/smelter negotiating range. However, smelting economics have deteriorated significantly over the past year due to lower acid and bonus metal credits as well as a decline in annual premia. Indeed, despite the rise in annual TC/RCs at the end of 2008, smelter production cuts have since been implemented in Japan, Kazakhstan, northern Europe and North America, thereby reducing the overall active capacity available to the market. _Mid-year negotiations are likely to be tough due to significant deterioration in smelting economics_ ### **BLISTER/ANODE AND SCRAP MARKETS** US scrap availability has been reported as a little easier over the past month, although volumes remain considerably lower in comparison with last year. Codelco, the world’s largest copper producer reported a 6.3% year-on-year increase in its Q1 2009 commercial copper output, to 390kt Cu.  The largest increase (39kt) was seen at the company’s new Gabriella Mistral division which was not in production during Q1 2008.  At the Nortй division production was 175kt in the January-March 2009 period (compared with 184kt a year earlier). Elsewhere, output at Salvador was 15kt (15kt), Andina 55kt (56kt) and El Teniente 88kt (93kt).  In addition, Codelco’s 49% share of El Abra production added a further 19kt (19kt).  Lower production at Codelco Nortй and El Teniente divisions resulted from declining ore grades (0.73% to 0.70% at the former and 0.98% to 0.93% at the latter). 

Following five years of preparation, BHP Billiton is seeking the approval of the Australian, South Australian and Northern Territory governments for a significant expansion of its existing mining and processing operation at Olympic Dam in northern South Australia.  BHP Billiton has delivered its environmental impact statement for the proposed expansion and the project schedule ultimately will depend on the timing and nature of government approvals and the final investment decision of the BHP Billiton Board.  Plans call for a progressive development over 11 years which would see mining rates raised from 12Mt/a to 72Mt/a.  At capacity, the new open pit mine and upgraded processing facilities would be capable of producing 2.4Mt/a of copper concentrates, 19kt/a of U3O8 plus gold and silver.  Surplus copper concentrates are likely to be smelted by third parties, most likely in China and the total refined copper output figure, including production via third parties, is put at 750kt/a Cu. 

Despite the closure of four mines (Akbastau, Abyz, Kounrad and Belouvsky) and cuts at a fifth (the West mine in Dzhezkazgan) in response to lower prices, Kazakhmys reported a 9% year-on-year increase in mined copper production in Q1 2009 (i.e. from 80.1kt to 87.4kt Cu).  The uplift was partly on account of good weather conditions at the start of this year and also due to higher output at a number of the company’s other mines (the total count being 21).  Kazakhmys also closed one of its two 125kt/a electric furnaces at Dzhezkazgan and this will remain shut until additional feed can be secured for the complex.  In the

In the interim, concentrates produced at Kazzinc’s Zyri

Zambia’s Luanshya Copper Mines (LCM) is to get a new lease of life once its acquisition by NFC Africa has been concluded.  J&W Investments shut the 24kt/a Baluba mine in December 2008 after it was deemed to be uneconomic. The Chinese acquirer will hold an 85% stake in the company with ZCCI retaining the balance.  Production is expected to resume in June and development work on the 60kt/a Muliashi SxEw project could be resumed before year end.  NFC is expected to invest $400M in the company and to reinstate 1,700 workers that were previously laid off when the mine shut. 

A recent uplift in copper prices has enabled Mopani Copper Mines to reverse its earlier decision to close its 60kt/a Mufulira mine and to place its 60kt/a Nkana operations onto care and maintenance.  The company had expected the latter to remain closed until prices recovered to ~$5000/t.  Separately, Mopani plans to develop a new open pit mine, known as Area D which is located within its Nkana lease area.  Plans call for the mining and extraction of 260kt of ore grading 4.22% Cu which would be treated in the existing Nkana concentrator. 

First Quantum Minerals (FQM) aims to restart its 50kt/a Bwana Mkubwa SxEw facility once it receives clearance to open a new mine, known as Fishtie in central Zambia.  The company has already filed an environmental assessment report with the Environmental Council of Zambia.  Identified reserves are apparently sufficient to sustain mining operations for approximately 27 months at a rate of 100kt/m.  The Bwana Mkubwa plant was shut down in October 2008 after it ran out of feed from the company’s Lonshi open pit.  Exports of ores had been banned by DRC authorities at the end of 2007.  FQM is considering an option to go underground at Lonshi to produce ~35kt/a of copper-in-concentrates.  Elsewhere the construction period of the 35kt/a Kolwezi Tailings project has been extended through to mid 2010 because of the company’s recent decision to reduce cash outflows.  At the end of Q1 2009 the project was 56% complete and FQM had invested $228M out of a total capital expenditure of $553M. 

Following a recent ruling by a Mexican Government entity, Southern Copper is considering reopening its 180kt/a Cananea mine by the start of 2010.  A Mexican labour board ruled that the mine could be officially closed enabling the company to fire striking workers because of damage that had been caused to equipment.  Southern Copper expects the repairs to cost ~$50M and take at least four months to complete.  However, the union has lodged an appeal against this decision and the company will not commit to restarting the mine pending a favourable response to the appeal.
